teach:
Week 1 Science: Science Practices — Questions, Hypotheses, Variables, Controls, and Experiment Design

Objectives

  • Turn an observation into a testable scientific question and write a hypothesis in "If…, then…, because…" form.
  • Identify the independent, dependent, and controlled variables in an experiment description.
  • Identify the control group and explain why it is needed.
  • Judge whether an experiment is a fair test (one variable changed, repeated trials, random assignment, no confounding variables).
  • Answer GED-style questions based on experiment descriptions and data tables.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors.
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Index cards (one per student) for the DRY MIX memory card.
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Testable or not? Sort four statements; turn one into a hypothesis.
Direct instruction20Questions, hypotheses, variables (DRY MIX), control groups, fair tests; Worked Examples 1–3.
Guided practice15The calm-music study: students identify every part of the design with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket and study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these four statements on the board. Ask: "Which ones could a scientist answer by running an experiment and collecting measurements?"

  1. Chocolate ice cream is the best flavor.
  2. Does salt water freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water?
  3. Do houseplants grow taller when they are watered with coffee?
  4. Are cats more beautiful than dogs?

Answers: 2 and 3 are testable. Each one names something we can change (salt or no salt; coffee or plain water) and something we can measure (freezing temperature; plant height). Statements 1 and 4 are opinions; there is no measurement that settles them.

Quick extension: Ask students to turn #2 into a prediction. Expected answer: "If salt is added to water, then the water will freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water." (This is correct: dissolved salt lowers the freezing point of water, which is why salt is spread on icy roads.)

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Science starts with a question. Scientists notice something (an observation) and ask a question about it. A good scientific question is testable: it names one thing to change and one thing to measure. "Does the temperature of water affect how fast sugar dissolves?" is testable. "Why is sugar so good?" is not.

2. A hypothesis is a testable prediction. It is not a wild guess and it is not a question. Teach the frame:

If [I change this], then [this measured result will happen], because [reason].

Example: If water is warmer, then a sugar cube will dissolve faster, because water particles move faster at higher temperatures and break the sugar apart more quickly.

Stress that data support or do not support a hypothesis; scientists do not say one experiment "proves" it.

3. Variables. A variable is anything that can change in an experiment.

  • Independent variable (IV): the one factor the scientist deliberately changes. It is the "cause" being tested.
  • Dependent variable (DV): what the scientist measures to see the effect. It "depends" on the independent variable.
  • Controlled variables (constants): everything else that is kept the same so it cannot affect the result.

Hand out index cards and have students write the memory aid DRY MIX:

Dependent variable = Responding variable = graphed on the Y-axis.
Manipulated variable = Independent variable = graphed on the X-axis.

4. Control group vs. controlled variables. These sound alike but differ. The control group does not get the treatment (or gets the normal condition); it is the baseline. The experimental groups get the treatment. Controlled variables are conditions kept the same for all groups. Without a control group, we cannot tell whether the treatment did anything.

5. What makes a fair test.

  • Change only one independent variable at a time.
  • Use repeated trials or a large enough sample so one unusual result does not mislead you. Average (mean) the trials.
  • In studies with people or animals, randomly assign subjects to groups so the groups start out alike.
  • Watch for confounding variables: a second difference between groups that could also explain the result.
  • In human studies, a placebo (a fake treatment that looks real) and keeping subjects unaware of their group help prevent expectations from affecting the results.

6. Conclusions. A conclusion says whether the data support the hypothesis and describes the pattern. It must stay within the data: a test from 10 °C to 55 °C says little about 100 °C.

Worked Example 1 — Identify the parts of an experiment

Scenario: A student wants to know whether the brand of paper towel affects how much water it absorbs. She cuts one 10 cm × 10 cm square from each of three brands (A, B, and C), dips each square into a bowl of room-temperature water for 10 seconds, lets it drip for 30 seconds, then squeezes the water into a measuring cup and records the volume. She repeats this three times for each brand.

Solution:

  • Question: Does the brand of paper towel affect how much water it absorbs?
  • Independent variable: brand of paper towel (A, B, or C).
  • Dependent variable: volume of water absorbed (mL).
  • Controlled variables: size of the square, time in the water, drip time, water temperature, method of squeezing.
  • Control group: none; she is comparing brands to one another. Not every experiment has a "no treatment" group.
  • Why three trials per brand? So one unusual square does not decide the result; she should use the mean.

Worked Example 2 — Write a hypothesis and find the control group

Scenario: A fitness coach asks whether 5 minutes of jumping jacks raises heart rate. Twenty adults are randomly split into two groups of 10. Group 1 does jumping jacks for 5 minutes. Group 2 sits quietly for 5 minutes. Each person's heart rate (beats per minute) is measured right afterward.

Solution:

  • Hypothesis: If a person does 5 minutes of jumping jacks, then the person's heart rate will be higher than if the person sat quietly, because working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.
  • Independent variable: activity (jumping jacks or sitting).
  • Dependent variable: heart rate in beats per minute.
  • Control group: Group 2, the people who sit quietly. They show what heart rate looks like without the exercise.
  • Controlled variables: length of time (5 minutes), when and how heart rate is measured, same room.
  • Why random assignment? So both groups have similar fitness levels and ages, and differ only in the activity.

Worked Example 3 — Spot the flaw and fix it

Scenario: A homeowner tests a new lawn fertilizer. He spreads it on his front lawn, which gets full sun all day, and spreads nothing on his back lawn, which is shaded by trees. After 4 weeks the front lawn is greener and thicker. He concludes the fertilizer works.

Solution:

  • Independent variable: fertilizer or no fertilizer. Dependent variable: how green and thick the grass is.
  • Flaw: the two lawns also differ in sunlight. Sunlight is a confounding variable. The front lawn might be greener because of the sun, not the fertilizer.
  • Fix: Use one lawn with even sunlight. Mark off several equal plots, randomly choose half to fertilize, and leave the other half unfertilized as the control. Water all plots the same. Measure each plot the same way (for example, count grass blades in a small square) and compare averages.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Read aloud. Students answer on paper; call on volunteers, then reveal.

Scenario: A nurse wonders whether listening to calm music lowers blood pressure in patients waiting for minor surgery. Sixty patients agree to take part. The nurse randomly assigns 30 patients to listen to calm music through headphones for 20 minutes. The other 30 wear the same headphones for 20 minutes with no sound playing. Each patient's blood pressure is measured just before and just after the 20 minutes.

  1. What question is being tested?
  2. Write a hypothesis using If…then…because.
  3. What is the independent variable?
  4. What is the dependent variable?
  5. Which group is the control group?
  6. Why does the control group wear headphones with no sound instead of no headphones?
  7. Why were patients randomly assigned?
  8. Name two controlled variables.

Answers:

  1. Does listening to calm music lower blood pressure in patients before surgery?
  2. If patients listen to calm music for 20 minutes, then their blood pressure will drop more than patients who hear no music, because calm music helps the body relax.
  3. Whether the patient hears calm music.
  4. Change in blood pressure.
  5. The 30 patients who wear headphones with no sound.
  6. So the only difference between the groups is the music. Wearing headphones and resting quietly might relax people by itself; this way, that effect is the same in both groups.
  7. So the groups start out similar (age, health, nervousness), which prevents a confounding variable.
  8. Any two: time (20 minutes), type of headphones, timing of measurements, measuring equipment.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–12 on the course page while you circulate. Unfinished items become homework.

Checks for Understanding (use during the wrap-up)

  • "What do you change on purpose?" Expected: the independent variable.
  • "What do you measure?" Expected: the dependent variable.
  • "Which axis gets the independent variable?" Expected: the x-axis (DRY MIX).
  • "What is the difference between a control group and a controlled variable?" Expected: the control group is a group that gets no treatment (the baseline); controlled variables are conditions kept the same for every group.
  • "Why repeat trials?" Expected: so one unusual result does not mislead us.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Swapping the IV and DV. Students often pick the most interesting variable. Correction: ask "Which one did the scientist choose ahead of time?" That is the independent variable. "Which one did the scientist have to wait and measure?" That is the dependent variable.

Confusing "control group" with "controlled variables." Correction: a control group is people, plants, or objects; controlled variables are conditions like temperature or time. Point to each in an example.

Writing the hypothesis as a question. "Does fertilizer help plants grow?" is the question. Correction: require the If…then form, which forces a prediction.

Missing a confounding variable. Students accept a conclusion because it sounds reasonable. Correction: train the habit of asking, "Besides the independent variable, how else were the groups different?"

Saying "proves" or going beyond the data. Correction: use "supports" or "does not support," and check that every part of a chosen conclusion is shown in the table or graph.

Differentiation

Support: Give sentence frames ("The scientist changed ____. The scientist measured ____. The scientist kept ____ the same."). Have students underline what is changed in one color and circle what is measured in another. Start with experiments that have only two groups before moving to multi-group tables. Let students keep the DRY MIX card out during practice.

Stretch: Have students design a complete experiment for a question of their choice (for example, "Does the color of a car affect how hot the inside gets?"), listing IV, DV, three controlled variables, the control group, and the number of trials. Or have them find a news headline that claims one thing causes another and name a possible confounding variable.

How This Shows Up on the GED

Many GED Science questions begin with a short experiment description, often with a table or graph, and ask about the design. Expect wording like:

  • "Which variable is the independent variable in this experiment?"
  • "Which hypothesis was the student most likely testing?"
  • "What is the purpose of the group that received no treatment?"
  • "Which change would most improve the reliability of the results?"
  • "Which conclusion is best supported by the data?"

Formats include multiple choice, drop-down menus that complete a statement, drag-and-drop sorting (for example, sorting factors into independent, dependent, and controlled), fill-in-the-blank (often a mean calculated from trials), and hot spots (clicking a sentence or a part of a figure). An on-screen calculator is available on the Science test. Teach students this routine for every experiment stimulus: (1) find what was changed, (2) find what was measured, (3) find what was kept the same and which group is the control, (4) then read the questions.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above, then preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's practice GED.

Science Practices: How Scientists Ask and Test Questions

On the GED Science test, you will read about experiments and studies and answer questions about how they were set up and what they show. You do not need to memorize lots of facts to do this well. You need a short list of ideas and a routine. This lesson gives you both.

1. Start with a testable question

Science begins with an observation: something you notice. Then you ask a question about it. A scientific question must be testable. That means you can change something and measure what happens.

  • Testable: "Does the temperature of water affect how fast sugar dissolves?"
  • Not testable: "Is summer the nicest season?" (That is an opinion.)

2. Write a hypothesis

A hypothesis is a testable prediction that answers your question. A useful pattern:

If [what you change], then [what you expect to measure], because [your reason].

Example: If water is warmer, then a sugar cube will dissolve faster, because water particles move faster when they are warmer.

After the experiment, the results either support the hypothesis or do not support it. Scientists do not say one experiment "proves" a hypothesis.

3. Know your variables

A variable is anything that can change in an experiment. There are three kinds you must recognize.

VariableWhat it isAsk yourself
IndependentThe one thing the scientist changes on purpose"What did they choose to change?"
DependentWhat the scientist measures; the result"What did they measure?"
ControlledEverything kept the same"What stayed the same for every group?"

Memory aid: DRY MIX. Dependent = Responding = Y-axis. Manipulated = Independent = X-axis. You can also say: "the effect of [independent] on [dependent]."

4. The control group

The control group does not get the treatment being tested (or gets the normal condition). It is the baseline you compare against. The groups that do get the treatment are the experimental groups.

Do not mix up the control group (a group of plants, people, or objects) with controlled variables (conditions like time, temperature, or amount of water that stay the same).

5. What makes a fair test

  • Change only one variable. If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused the result.
  • Repeat trials or use many subjects. One plant or one person can be unusual. Find the mean (average) of several trials.
  • Randomly assign subjects to groups so the groups start out alike.
  • Watch for confounding variables: any second difference between groups that could explain the result.
  • In studies with people, use a placebo (a fake treatment that looks real), so expectations do not affect the results.

6. Draw a conclusion

A conclusion tells what the data show and whether they support the hypothesis. Stay inside the data. If the experiment tested water from 10 °C to 55 °C, do not make claims about boiling water.

Worked Examples

Example 1. A student fills three identical cups with 200 mL of water at 10 °C, 30 °C, and 50 °C. She drops one sugar cube into each cup without stirring and times how long it takes to dissolve.

Step 1, what changed? Water temperature → independent variable.
Step 2, what was measured? Time to dissolve → dependent variable.
Step 3, what stayed the same? Cup, amount of water, size of cube, no stirring → controlled variables.
Improvement: She should repeat each temperature at least three times and find the mean.

Example 2. A researcher randomly divides 40 tomato plants into two groups. Group A gets a new plant food. Group B gets plain water. Everything else is the same. After 6 weeks she counts the tomatoes on each plant.

Hypothesis: If tomato plants get the new plant food, then they will produce more tomatoes than plants given plain water, because the plant food supplies nutrients the plants need.
Independent variable: plant food or no plant food. Dependent variable: number of tomatoes. Control group: Group B (plain water).

Example 3. A company tests a new energy bar. Ten professional cyclists eat the bar; ten people who never exercise eat a plain cracker. Then everyone rides a stationary bike as long as they can. The cyclists ride much longer.

What is wrong? The groups differ in fitness, not just in what they ate. Fitness is a confounding variable, so we cannot say the bar caused the difference. Fix: Choose people from the same population and randomly assign them to the two groups. Give the second group a bar that looks and tastes the same but lacks the special ingredients (a placebo).

Try It

1. A student asks, "Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall sunflowers grow?" Write a hypothesis.

Show answer

Sample: If sunflowers get more hours of sunlight each day, then they will grow taller, because plants use light energy to make their food. Any answer that predicts how sunlight (the change) affects height (the measurement) is correct.

2. In a study, people drank 0, 1, 2, or 3 cups of coffee and then their reaction time was measured. Name the independent and dependent variables.

Show answer

Independent variable: number of cups of coffee. Dependent variable: reaction time.

3. A scientist tests whether a new soap kills more bacteria. Some plates get the new soap, some get regular soap, and some get only water. Which plates are the control group?

Show answer

The plates that get only water. They show how many bacteria survive with no soap at all. (The regular soap plates are a useful comparison too, but the water-only plates are the no-treatment baseline.)

4. A student tests whether ball size affects how far it rolls. She rolls a small ball on carpet and a large ball on tile. What is wrong with this test?

Show answer

She changed two variables at once: ball size and floor surface. The surface is a confounding variable. Both balls should roll on the same surface.

5. A student's three trials for drying time were 12, 15, and 18 minutes. What is the mean?

Show answer

(12 + 15 + 18) ÷ 3 = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 minutes.
post:
Post Lesson: Science Practices

Summary of Key Points

  • A scientific question is testable: you can change something and measure the result.
  • A hypothesis is a testable prediction. Use "If…, then…, because…." Data support or do not support it.
  • The independent variable is what the scientist changes (x-axis). The dependent variable is what is measured (y-axis). Controlled variables are kept the same.
  • The control group gets no treatment (or the normal condition) and is the baseline for comparison.
  • A fair test changes one variable, repeats trials, uses random assignment, and avoids confounding variables.
  • Conclusions must stay within the data that were actually collected.

Exit Ticket

1. A runner tests whether the type of shoe affects her time to run one mile. What is the dependent variable?

Show answer

Her time to run one mile.

2. Rewrite this question as a hypothesis: "Does adding salt to water change its boiling point?"

Show answer

Sample: If salt is added to water, then the water will boil at a higher temperature, because the dissolved salt makes it harder for water particles to escape as vapor. (Dissolved salt does raise the boiling point slightly.)

3. True or false: The control group and the controlled variables mean the same thing.

Show answer

False. The control group is a group that gets no treatment. Controlled variables are conditions kept the same for all groups.

4. A study of a new medicine gave the medicine to young volunteers and a sugar pill to older volunteers. What is the main problem?

Show answer

Age is a confounding variable. The groups differ in age as well as treatment, so we cannot tell which caused any difference. Volunteers should be randomly assigned.

5. On a graph of your results, which variable goes on the x-axis?

Show answer

The independent variable (DRY MIX: Manipulated, Independent, X-axis).

Reflection

  • Which idea from this lesson felt the most natural to you, and which one do you still mix up?
  • Think of something you noticed this week at home or work. What testable question could you ask about it, and what would your independent and dependent variables be?
  • When you read a claim like "People who drink green tea live longer," what confounding variable might explain it?

Day 2Complete practice items 1–6. For each one you miss, read the explanation and write one sentence about why the right answer is right. (30 min)
Day 3Complete practice items 7–12. Study the vocabulary list until you can define each term from memory. (30 min)

Day 6Review every practice GED question you missed. Sort your mistakes by type (variables, data, conclusions) and reread that part of the lesson. (30–40 min)

Test-Taking Strategy: Label Before You Answer

When a GED Science question describes an experiment, do not jump to the answer choices. First jot three quick labels on your scratch paper: C (what was changed), M (what was measured), and S (what stayed the same, including the control group). It takes about 20 seconds and makes most design questions easy, because the wrong answer choices usually swap these roles.

notes:
Study Notes: Science Practices

The Steps

  1. Observation: notice something.
  2. Question: must be testable.
  3. Hypothesis: If…, then…, because…
  4. Experiment: change one variable; control the rest.
  5. Data: measure, repeat trials, find the mean.
  6. Conclusion: data support / do not support the hypothesis.

DRY MIX

Dependent = Responding = Y-axis
Manipulated = Independent = X-axis

Check: "The effect of [IV] on [DV]."

Fair Test Checklist

  • Only one independent variable changes.
  • Controlled variables are the same for all groups.
  • There is a control group (baseline) when possible.
  • Several trials or many subjects per group.
  • Subjects are randomly assigned.
  • No confounding variable (no second difference between groups).
  • Human studies: placebo; subjects do not know their group.
TermMeaningSugar-cube example
Independent variableWhat is changed on purposeWater temperature
Dependent variableWhat is measuredTime to dissolve
Controlled variablesKept the sameWater volume, cube size, no stirring
Control groupNo treatment; baselineRoom-temperature water (if testing heated vs. not heated)
Confounding variableA second difference that could explain resultsStirring only the warm cup

Mean of trials: add the trials, divide by the number of trials. Example: (80 + 84 + 82) ÷ 3 = 82.

Watch out: control group ≠ controlled variables. Never say "proves." Do not conclude beyond the range of data tested.

items.prompt: What is the independent variable in this experiment?
options: The amount of fertilizer each plant received per week
The mean height of the plants after 21 days
The amount of water each plant received
The number of plants in each group
items.hint: The independent variable is the one thing the student changed on purpose from group to group.
items.explain:
The student deliberately gave each group a different amount of fertilizer (0, 5, 10, 15, or 20 mL per week), so fertilizer amount is the independent variable.

Plant height is what she measured, so it is the dependent variable, not the independent one. The water amount and the number of plants per group were kept the same for every group, so they are controlled variables.

items.prompt: Which group served as the control group?
options: Group 1, which received 0 mL of fertilizer per week
Group 3, which received 10 mL of fertilizer per week
Group 4, which grew the tallest plants
Group 5, which received the most fertilizer
items.hint: A control group does not receive the treatment being tested.
items.explain:
The treatment being tested is fertilizer. Group 1 received no fertilizer, so it shows how the plants grow without the treatment. That makes it the baseline, or control group.

Group 4 grew the tallest plants, but that is a result, not a reason to call it the control. Groups 2–5 all received fertilizer, so they are experimental groups.

items.prompt: Read Maria's lab notebook entry. Click the sentence that states Maria's hypothesis.
spans: Maria noticed that bread kept on top of her refrigerator grew mold faster than bread kept in a cupboard.
She wondered whether temperature affects how quickly mold grows on bread.
She checked with a thermometer and found that the top of the refrigerator was about 5 °C warmer than the cupboard.
If bread is stored at a warmer temperature, then visible mold will appear on it sooner than on bread stored at a cooler temperature.
She sealed identical slices of the same brand of bread in plastic bags and kept them at 10 °C, 20 °C, and 30 °C.
Each day she recorded whether mold was visible on each slice.
items.hint: A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested. Look for an If…then statement.
items.explain:
The hypothesis is the testable prediction: "If bread is stored at a warmer temperature, then visible mold will appear on it sooner…" It names what will be changed (temperature) and what will be measured (when mold appears).

The sentence "She wondered whether temperature affects how quickly mold grows" is Maria's question, not her hypothesis; it does not make a prediction. The first sentence is an observation, the third is a measurement she made, and the last two describe the procedure.

items.prompt: Sort each factor from the bean plant experiment into the correct category.
choices: Height of each plant after 21 days
items.hint: Ask: What was changed? What was measured? What was kept the same for every group?
items.explain:
• Independent variable: amount of fertilizer per week; it was changed on purpose (0 to 20 mL).
  • Dependent variable: plant height after 21 days; it was measured to see the effect.
  • Controlled variables: water (100 mL every other day), potting soil (the same for all pots), and light (12 hours per day from the same lamp) were kept the same so they could not cause differences in height.

A common mistake is to put height in the independent column because it is the most interesting result. Height is what the student waited to measure, so it is dependent.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: Mean plant height increased as fertilizer increased from 0 to 15 mL per week, but it was lower at 20 mL than at 15 mL.
Every increase in fertilizer produced taller plants.
Plants given 20 mL of fertilizer per week were shorter than plants given no fertilizer.
The amount of fertilizer had no effect on plant height.
items.hint: Read the heights in order from 0 mL to 20 mL. Does the height go up every time?
items.explain:
Mean heights in order: 12.0 → 15.5 → 19.0 → 21.5 cm (rising from 0 to 15 mL), then 18.0 cm at 20 mL (lower than 21.5). So height rose up to 15 mL and then dropped.

"Every increase produced taller plants" is wrong because the step from 15 to 20 mL went down. The 20 mL plants (18.0 cm) were still taller than the 0 mL plants (12.0 cm), so that choice is false. Heights clearly changed across groups, so fertilizer did have an effect.

items.prompt: Why did the student grow four plants in each group instead of just one?
options: Using several plants reduces the chance that one unusual plant will distort the results.
Using several plants makes each plant grow faster.
Using several plants allows the student to test more than one independent variable.
Using several plants means a control group is not needed.
items.hint: Think about what could happen if the only plant in a group had a weak seed.
items.explain:
Individual plants vary. If a group had only one plant and its seed happened to be weak, that group's result would be misleading. Averaging four plants makes the result more reliable.

The number of plants does not change how fast each plant grows, does not add a second independent variable, and does not replace the need for a control group (Group 1 is still needed as the baseline).

items.prompt: What is the mean time, in seconds, for the sugar cube to dissolve in 40 °C water? Enter a number.
items.hint: Add the three trials at 40 °C, then divide by 3.
items.explain:
Trials at 40 °C: 80 s, 84 s, 82 s.

80 + 84 + 82 = 246

246 ÷ 3 = 82 seconds

A common error is to add the trials and forget to divide (246), or to divide by 4 instead of 3.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement about the dissolving experiment.

In this experiment, the independent variable is {{0}}, and the dependent variable is {{1}}. The data show that as water temperature increases, the time needed for the sugar cube to dissolve {{2}}.

options: the water temperature
the time to dissolve
the size of the sugar cube
the volume of water
the water temperature
the time to dissolve
the size of the sugar cube
the volume of water
increases
decreases
stays the same

items.hint: The student chose the temperatures ahead of time and used a timer to measure the result.
items.explain:
The student set the water temperature (10, 25, 40, 55 °C), so it is the independent variable. She measured the time to dissolve with a timer, so it is the dependent variable. Cube size and water volume (200 mL) were held constant, so they are controlled variables.

The mean times fall from 182 s to 121 s to 82 s to 53 s as temperature rises, so the time decreases. (Warmer water dissolves sugar faster, which means less time.)

items.prompt: The student plans one more set of trials using water at 70 °C. Based on the trend in the data, which range most likely contains the mean dissolving time at 70 °C?
options: Between 25 and 45 seconds
Between 55 and 75 seconds
Between 80 and 100 seconds
Between 180 and 200 seconds
items.hint: Every 15 °C increase has made the time shorter. By how much did it drop each time?
items.explain:
Mean times: 182 s (10 °C), 121 s (25 °C), 82 s (40 °C), 53 s (55 °C). Each 15 °C step lowered the time, by 61 s, then 39 s, then 29 s. The drops are getting smaller, so the next drop should be smaller than 29 s, perhaps about 20 s. That predicts roughly 53 − 20 ≈ 33 s, which is in the range 25 to 45 seconds.

Every other range is at or above 53 s, which would mean the trend reversed and warmer water dissolved sugar more slowly. Nothing in the data suggests that.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the company's conclusion is not supported by this study?
options: The two groups differed in fitness level as well as in what they drank, so the drink may not have caused the difference.
Group B drank water instead of drinking nothing at all.
The volunteers ran on a treadmill instead of an outdoor track.
Endurance was measured in minutes instead of in miles.
items.hint: Besides the drink, how else were Group A and Group B different?
items.explain:
Group A was made up of college athletes and Group B of people who rarely exercise. Athletes would likely run longer no matter what they drank. Fitness level is a confounding variable, so the study cannot show that the drink caused the longer running time.

Giving the control group water is a reasonable choice, and running on a treadmill or measuring time in minutes are acceptable methods applied equally to both groups. None of those explains the large difference the way the fitness difference does.

items.prompt: Which two changes would make the sports drink study a fairer test of whether the drink improves endurance? Select two answers.
options: Choose all volunteers from one population and randomly assign them to the two groups.
Give Group B a drink that looks and tastes like the sports drink but lacks its active ingredients, and do not tell volunteers which drink they received.
Let each volunteer choose which drink he or she prefers.
Have Group A run on a treadmill and Group B run on an outdoor track.
Tell Group A that the sports drink is expected to improve their endurance.
items.hint: A fair test makes the groups as alike as possible except for the one thing being tested.
items.explain:
Random assignment from one population makes the two groups similar in fitness, age, and other traits, removing the confounding variable. A placebo drink that looks and tastes the same, with volunteers not knowing their group, keeps expectations from affecting how long people run.

Letting volunteers choose their drink lets other differences creep back in (for example, fitter people might choose the sports drink). Running in different places adds a second variable. Telling Group A what to expect could make them try harder, which biases the results.

items.prompt: A student wants to test whether the number of hours of light per day affects the growth of bean plants. Which plan is the best experimental design?
options: Grow four groups of five plants under 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving every plant the same water, the same soil, and 10 mL of fertilizer per week.
Grow four groups of five plants under 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving the groups 5, 10, 15, and 20 mL of fertilizer per week, respectively.
Grow one plant under each of 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving every plant the same water, the same soil, and 10 mL of fertilizer per week.
Grow four groups of five plants under 12 hours of light per day, giving each group a different amount of water.
items.hint: The best plan changes only the light, keeps everything else the same, and uses more than one plant per condition.
items.explain:
The best plan changes only the hours of light (the independent variable), keeps water, soil, and fertilizer the same (controlled variables), and uses five plants per group so the results are reliable.

The plan that gives the groups 5, 10, 15, and 20 mL of fertilizer changes light and fertilizer at the same time, so any difference could come from either one. The plan with one plant per condition lets a single unusual plant distort the results. The plan that keeps every group at 12 hours of light and changes the water does not test light at all.
